VM vs Batch Comparison

Azure Deployment Comparison¶

This document helps you choose between Azure VM and Azure Batch deployment options for Crackz.

Quick Decision Matrix¶

Criterion Azure VM Azure Batch
Dataset Size Small to medium (<1000 images) Large (1000+ images)
Processing Time Minutes to hours Hours to days
Parallelism Single instance Multiple nodes (2-100+)
Cost Predictable (fixed VM cost) Variable (pay per compute time)
Setup Complexity Simple Moderate
Use Case Development, testing, small projects Production, batch processing, research
GUI Support Yes (RDP available) No (headless only)
Best For Interactive work, model development Large-scale automated processing

Azure VM Deployment¶

When to Use¶

  • Development & Testing: Interactive environment with RDP access
  • Small Datasets: Processing up to 1000 images
  • GUI Required: Need to use Crackz GUI for manual inspection
  • Predictable Costs: Fixed hourly rate for VM
  • Learning: Experimenting with Crackz features

Pros¶

✓ Simple setup (one script, one command)
✓ RDP access for interactive work
✓ Predictable hourly costs
✓ Full Windows environment
✓ Good for development and debugging

Cons¶

✗ Limited to single VM performance
✗ Manual scaling required
✗ Not cost-effective for large datasets
✗ Idle time still incurs costs

Example Usage¶

# Create Windows 11 VM
./scripts/azure/azure_vm.sh \
  --name crackz-dev \
  --size Standard_D4s_v3

# Connect via RDP and use GUI
# IP address displayed after creation

Cost Example¶

  • Standard_D4s_v3 (4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM): ~$0.20/hour
  • 8 hours of processing: ~$1.60
  • Monthly (730 hours): ~$146 if left running

Azure Batch Deployment¶

When to Use¶

  • Large Datasets: Processing thousands of images
  • Parallel Processing: Need to process multiple projects simultaneously
  • Cost Optimization: Want to pay only for actual compute time
  • Automation: Fully automated pipelines without human interaction
  • Scale: Need to scale from 2 to 100+ nodes dynamically

Pros¶

✓ Massive parallelism (100+ nodes)
✓ Pay only for compute time
✓ Automatic task distribution
✓ Low-priority VMs (up to 80% cost savings)
✓ Built-in retry and failure handling
✓ Integration with Azure Storage

Cons¶

✗ More complex setup
✗ Headless only (no GUI)
✗ Requires understanding of Batch concepts
✗ Initial learning curve

Example Usage¶

# Create batch pool with 10 nodes
./scripts/azure/azure_batch.sh \
  --batch-account mybatchaccount \
  --storage-account mystorage \
  --node-count 10 \
  --vm-size Standard_D4s_v3

# Submit 100 detection jobs
for i in {1..100}; do
  az batch task create \
    --job-id detection-job \
    --task-id "task-$i" \
    --command-line "docker run crackz-cli:latest detect run --project /data/project-$i"
done

Cost Example (10 nodes)¶

  • Standard_D4s_v3: ~$0.20/hour per node
  • 10 nodes for 2 hours: ~$4.00
  • Low-priority pricing: ~$0.80 (80% savings)

Hybrid Approach¶

For many workflows, combining both approaches works best:

Recommended Workflow¶

  1. Development Phase (Azure VM)
  2. Use VM for model development and tuning
  3. Test with small sample dataset
  4. Finalize configuration and parameters

  5. Export optimized project config

  6. Production Phase (Azure Batch)

  7. Deploy validated configuration to Batch
  8. Process full dataset in parallel
  9. Collect results in Azure Storage
  10. Analyze aggregated metrics

Example¶

# Phase 1: Development on VM
./scripts/azure/azure_vm.sh --name crackz-dev --size Standard_D4s_v3
# RDP in, use GUI to develop and test
# Export config: crackz export-config --project demo --out optimized.yaml

# Phase 2: Production on Batch
./scripts/azure/azure_batch.sh \
  --batch-account prod-batch \
  --pool-id production-pool \
  --node-count 20 \
  --vm-size Standard_D8s_v3

# Upload optimized config and data to storage
# Submit batch jobs with optimized parameters

Feature Comparison¶

Feature Azure VM Azure Batch
Deployment Script azure_vm.sh azure_batch.sh
Max Parallelism 1 Unlimited
Docker Support Manual Native
Auto-scaling No Yes
Task Retry Manual Automatic
Job Dependencies Manual Built-in
Output Collection Manual Automatic
Monitoring Azure Portal Batch API + Portal
Storage Integration Manual mount Native

Cost Optimization Tips¶

For Azure VM¶

  1. Use B-series for development (burstable, cheaper)
  2. Stop VM when not in use (only pay for storage)
  3. Use spot instances for non-critical work (up to 90% savings)
  4. Resize VM based on workload

For Azure Batch¶

  1. Use low-priority VMs for fault-tolerant workloads
  2. Enable auto-scaling to scale down when idle
  3. Delete pools when not needed
  4. Use smaller VM sizes with higher node counts
  5. Batch similar tasks to reduce overhead

Getting Started¶

First Time Users¶

  1. Start with Azure VM to learn Crackz
  2. Process small sample dataset
  3. Understand the workflow and configuration
  4. Graduate to Azure Batch for production

Experienced Users¶

  • Use Azure VM for:
  • Model experimentation
  • Configuration tuning
  • Small ad-hoc jobs

  • GUI-based analysis

  • Use Azure Batch for:

  • Production pipelines
  • Large dataset processing
  • Automated workflows
  • Cost-sensitive operations

Migration Path¶

Moving from VM to Batch:

# 1. Develop on VM
./scripts/azure/azure_vm.sh --name dev-vm

# 2. Test configuration
crackz detect train --project my-project --epochs 50
crackz detect run --project my-project

# 3. Export configuration
crackz export-config --project my-project --out batch-config.yaml

# 4. Upload to Azure Storage
az storage blob upload-batch \
  --account-name mystorage \
  --destination crackz-data \
  --source my-project

# 5. Create Batch pool
./scripts/azure/azure_batch.sh \
  --batch-account mybatch \
  --storage-account mystorage \
  --node-count 10

# 6. Submit batch jobs
az batch job create --id production-job --pool-id crackz-pool
# ... add tasks

Support and Documentation¶

  • Azure VM: See scripts/azure/azure_vm.sh --help
  • Azure Batch: See Azure Batch Documentation
  • Configuration: See Configuration Reference
  • Docker Images: See Docker Usage

FAQ¶

Q: Can I use GPU with both options?
A: Yes. Use --size Standard_NC* for VM, and similar for Batch pool config.

Q: Which is faster for 5000 images?
A: Batch with 20 nodes can be 20x faster than single VM.

Q: Can I use both simultaneously?
A: Yes! Develop on VM, process on Batch.

Q: What about costs for idle time?
A: VM charges for uptime. Batch only charges for task execution time.

Q: Can I access Batch task outputs?
A: Yes, via Azure Storage or download with az batch task file download.

Advanced Performance

Advanced Performance & Reproducibility¶

This page describes optional settings for faster training / inference and more reproducible runs.

Overview¶

Advanced knobs live under ai.training and ai.detection in the project YAML (or unified ProjectConfig). They are all optional and default to safe, CPU‑friendly values.

Area Field Location Purpose
Precision precision ai.training Mixed precision / bfloat16 acceleration
Devices devices ai.training Number of devices (GPUs) for distributed training
Strategy strategy ai.training PyTorch Lightning strategy (e.g. ddp)
Reproducibility seed ai.training, ai.detection Sets global RNGs (python/numpy/torch/lightning)

Mixed Precision¶

Mixed precision can significantly improve throughput on modern GPUs.

Supported values (Lightning compatible): - 16 or 16-mixed – FP16 mixed precision - bf16-mixed – bfloat16 mixed precision (Ampere + some CPUs) - 32 – (default if omitted)

Example: 

ai:
  training:
    precision: 16-mixed
    batch_size: 16
CLI run: 
crackz detect train --project demo-project
(Precision is read from project YAML; no extra flag required.)

Multi-GPU / Distributed Training¶

Enable multi-GPU training by specifying devices > 1 and a suitable strategy (usually ddp).

ai:
  training:
    devices: 2
    strategy: ddp
    batch_size: 8
    precision: bf16-mixed

Run (assuming 2 visible GPUs): 

crackz detect train --project demo-project

Docker (GPU): 

docker run --gpus all --rm -v %cd%\project:/home/app crackz-cli:gpu \
  detect train --project /home/app/demo-project

Strategies Cheat Sheet¶

Strategy Use Case Notes
ddp Standard multi-GPU Best default on Linux
ddp_spawn Windows / Jupyter Slight overhead
auto Let Lightning decide Conservative choice

Seeding & Reproducibility¶

Set seed in either training or detection sections: 

ai:
  training:
    seed: 1234
  detection:
    seed: 1234
Effect: - Sets PYTHONHASHSEED, python random, numpy, torch (CPU + CUDA), and Lightning worker seeds. - Does NOT force deterministic convolution algorithms (can slow performance). Add those manually if needed: 
import torch
torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)

Caveats¶

  • GPU kernels may still introduce nondeterminism (atomic ops, etc.).
  • Different hardware / driver stacks can still change results slightly.

Example Comprehensive YAML¶

project:
  name: demo-project
  description: Perf tuned
paths:
  project_path: demo-project
  image_path: demo-project/images
  image_mask_path: demo-project/masks
  artifacts_path: demo-project/artifacts
logging:
  level: INFO
  log_dir: logs
ai:
  model:
    encoder: resnet34
    device: cuda
    input_size: [512, 512]
    threshold: 0.5
  training:
    batch_size: 16
    epochs: 20
    learning_rate: 0.0005
    precision: 16-mixed
    devices: 2
    strategy: ddp
    seed: 4242
  detection:
    batch_size: 8
    seed: 4242

Workflow Tips¶

Goal Tip
Prototype quickly Keep CPU defaults; small batch, epochs=1, precision unset
Throughput Increase batch_size gradually; enable 16-mixed precision
Large model memory Use bf16-mixed (if supported) or reduce batch_size
Reproducible baseline Fix seed; export config (crackz export-config)

Exporting a Tuned Config¶

After modifying fields inside the project YAML: 

crackz export-config --project demo-project --out tuned_config.yaml
Share tuned_config.yaml for reproducible runs.

Detection Phase Seeds¶

Providing ai.detection.seed ensures preprocessing ordering / transforms (if later added) are deterministic between runs.

Troubleshooting¶

Issue Suggestion
OOM errors Lower batch_size or remove mixed precision
Slower than expected Ensure CUDA visible; confirm precision active in logs
DDP hang Use ddp_spawn on Windows or for notebook contexts
Seed ineffective Check for non-deterministic ops; set torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)

Migration Guide

Project Schema Migration¶

Crackz versions project YAML files with a simple integer schema_version field. When new optional fields are added (e.g. ai.training.tensorboard) the schema version increases and a lightweight in-place migration is available.

When Migration Is Needed¶

You may need migration if: - Your project YAML has no schema_version field (legacy v0) - The value is lower than the current CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION exposed by crackz.project.migration

Migration adds any missing defaulted fields and stamps the new schema_version. It never removes user data.

Schema Version History¶

Version Changes Notes
0 (legacy) No schema_version field, no ai.training.tensorboard Original projects created before versioning
1 Added schema_version: 1 and ai.training.tensorboard: false First versioned schema
2 Added data section with mask_threshold: 1 Binary mask conversion support
3 New artifacts structure + project.crackz_version tracking Current version - Improved organization

Version 3 Changes (Current)¶

Schema version 3 introduces improved artifacts organization and version tracking:

schema_version: 3
project:
  name: my_project
  description: My crack detection project
  created: '2025-01-15T10:30:00Z'
  crackz_version: '0.50.0'  # NEW: Tracks Crackz app version

What gets added: - project.crackz_version: Tracks which Crackz version created/last modified the project - New artifacts directory structure (backward compatible): - checkpoints/ to models/ (clearer purpose for model weights) - runtime/ for temporary artifacts (TensorBoard, Lightning logs) - detections/visualizations/ for PNG detection outputs

Backward compatibility: - Old projects continue working - checkpoints_path checks legacy checkpoints/ directory first - New writes automatically use improved structure (models/, runtime/, etc.) - File migration available - optionally migrate existing files to new structure - Migration only updates schema version and adds crackz_version field by default

Version 2 Changes¶

Schema version 2 introduced the data configuration section:

data:
  mask_threshold: 1
schema_version: 2

Added data.mask_threshold for binary mask conversion during image import.

CLI Auto / Assisted Migration¶

Most CLI commands that load a project (e.g. detect train, detect run, image imports, exporting configs, pruning checkpoints) now check the schema version and will:

  1. Interactive terminal:
  2. Prompt: Project schema v0 < v1. Migrate now? [y/N]:
  3. On Yes: Runs in-place migration with a .bak backup.
  4. Non-interactive (CI, pipelines):
  5. If CRACKZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=1 is set, migration runs automatically.
  6. Otherwise a guidance message is printed and the old schema is used.

Manual Migration Command¶

Use the explicit command to inspect or apply migrations:

crackz migrate --project <path-to-project-dir>
# or
crackz migrate --cfg <path-to-project-yaml>

Common flags: - --dry-run : Show what would change without writing. - --no-backup : Skip writing <file>.bak before overwrite. - --migrate-files : NEW Also migrate artifacts directory structure (checkpoints to models, etc.)

Schema-Only Migration (Default)¶

Basic migration only updates the YAML schema and adds missing fields:

# Using project directory
crackz migrate --project my_project --dry-run
crackz migrate --project my_project

# Using direct YAML file path
crackz migrate --cfg my_project/my_project_project.yaml

File Migration (Optional)¶

NEW in v3: Optionally migrate the actual artifacts directory structure:

# Preview what files would be moved
crackz migrate --project my_project --migrate-files --dry-run

# Migrate both schema AND files
crackz migrate --project my_project --migrate-files

File migration moves: - checkpoints/ to models/ - training/tensorboard/ to runtime/tensorboard/ - training/lightning_logs/ to runtime/lightning_logs/ - detections/*.png to detections/visualizations/

Safety features: - Always creates backup of entire artifacts directory before moving files - Interactive confirmation before proceeding - Automatic rollback if migration fails - Detailed progress reporting

Backups¶

By default, a timestamped backup is created before modifying the original project file. Backup files use the format: {filename}.v{version}.{timestamp}.bak

Example: 

myproject_project.v2.20250115_143022.bak

This format includes: - Version number (v2) - Shows which schema version this backup came from - Timestamp (20250115_143022) - UTC timestamp ensures unique backups per migration - Multiple migrations create multiple backups (never overwrites previous backups)

To revert a migration: 1. Locate the timestamped backup file (e.g., myproject_project.v2.20250115_143022.bak) 2. Remove or rename the current YAML file 3. Rename the backup file to remove the .v2.20250115_143022.bak suffix

Benefits: - Never lose migration history (each migration creates a unique backup) - Easy to identify which version a backup came from - Can rollback to any previous migration step if needed

Environment Variable Summary¶

Variable Effect
CRACKZ_AUTO_MIGRATE=1 Auto-migrate without prompt in non-interactive sessions

Programmatic Migration¶

You can call the library function directly:

from pathlib import Path
from crackz.project.migration import migrate_project_file

result = migrate_project_file(Path("my_project"))  # or path/to_yaml
print(result)
# Example result:
# {
#   'status': 'migrated',
#   'from_version': 2,
#   'to_version': 3,
#   'steps': ['2->3: updated to artifacts structure v3 + added crackz_version tracking'],
#   'path': 'my_project/my_project_project.yaml',
#   'backup_path': 'my_project/my_project_project.v2.20250115_143022.bak',
#   'dry_run': False
# }

The result dict contains: - status: "migrated", "noop", or "up-to-date" - from_version: Original schema version - to_version: Final schema version - steps: List of migration step descriptions - path: Path to migrated file - backup_path: Path to backup file (if created) - dry_run: Whether this was a dry run

GUI Migration¶

Automated Migration Detection¶

When opening a project in the GUI, automatic detection occurs for:

  1. Schema Migration: Always prompted and performed when project schema is outdated
  2. File Migration: Detects when artifacts directory structure needs updating

Schema Migration Dialog¶

When opening a project with an old schema version, the GUI displays a dialog offering migration. A backup is created automatically; declining leaves the project untouched.

File Migration Dialog (NEW)¶

When artifacts directory structure is outdated, the GUI displays an informational dialog explaining: - Benefits of the new structure (better organization, clearer separation) - Safety measures (backup creation, rollback capability) - User options: "Migrate", "Skip", or "Cancel"

The migration process shows progress and handles any errors gracefully with automatic rollback.

Safety and Idempotence¶

Running migration on an already up-to-date project is a no-op. Repeated runs after success make no further changes.

Troubleshooting¶

Symptom Cause Resolution
Prompt appears every run Write failed, read-only filesystem Ensure write permissions to project directory
Field still missing after migration Uncommitted manual edits reverted defaults Re-run migration or add field manually
Many .bak files accumulate Multiple migrations over time Safe to delete old backups after verifying current project works
Need to rollback migration Migration caused issues Rename timestamped .bak file to remove suffix and replace current YAML

Shell Completion

Shell Completion¶

Crackz uses Typer, which provides built-in shell completion generation for common shells. This page shows how to enable and verify completion for the crackz CLI.

Supported Shells¶

  • Bash
  • Zsh
  • Fish
  • PowerShell (Core / Windows)

Quick One-Off Completion (Any Shell)¶

You can preview completion script output without installing it permanently: 

crackz --show-completion bash
crackz --show-completion zsh
crackz --show-completion fish
crackz --show-completion powershell
Pipe it into source / Invoke-Expression for a temporary session (examples below).

Persistent Installation¶

Typer exposes a helper flag: 

crackz --install-completion SHELL
Replace SHELL with one of: bash, zsh, fish, powershell. After installation open a new shell (or source your updated profile) and test with: 
crackz det<TAB>
It should expand to: 
crackz detect

Bash¶

crackz --install-completion bash
# New shell OR
source ~/.bash_completion
If using Git Bash on Windows ensure bash-completion is available; otherwise fall back to --show-completion and manual sourcing.

Zsh¶

crackz --install-completion zsh
# Then restart shell or:
autoload -U compinit && compinit
If the script is placed in a directory not in $fpath, move it or append that location to fpath.

Fish¶

crackz --install-completion fish
# Typically installs into ~/.config/fish/completions/
# Reload:
exec fish

PowerShell (Windows / Cross‑Platform)¶

Recommended: Use the helper script we ship: 

pwsh -File scripts/setup_completion.ps1
# Or force re-install:
pwsh -File scripts/setup_completion.ps1 -Force
This will: 1. Ensure crackz is callable. 2. Run crackz --install-completion powershell. 3. Append an evaluation line to your PowerShell profile if missing: 
crackz --show-completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression
4. Instruct you to reload your session (. $PROFILE).

Manual (without script): 

crackz --install-completion powershell
# If the profile wasn't updated, add manually:
Add-Content $PROFILE "crackz --show-completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression"
. $PROFILE

Temporary Session Activation Examples¶

Shell Command
Bash crackz --show-completion bash > /tmp/crackz.sh && source /tmp/crackz.sh
Zsh source <(crackz --show-completion zsh)
Fish crackz --show-completion fish | source
PowerShell crackz --show-completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression

Troubleshooting¶

Symptom Possible Cause Resolution
No suggestions after install Profile not reloaded Open new shell or source profile (. $PROFILE)
Command not found Virtual env not active Activate venv or use uv run crackz --install-completion ... then adjust profile line to call uv run crackz --show-completion ...
Duplicate entries appended Script re-run without --Force cleanly Use -Force with the PowerShell helper or manually prune profile
Zsh errors about compinit compinit not initialized Run autoload -U compinit && compinit
Bash no _completion_loader found Missing bash-completion package Install bash-completion or source manually from --show-completion output

Uninstalling Completion¶

Manually remove the added line from your shell profile (e.g., ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, PowerShell $PROFILE) and delete any generated completion file (Fish: remove from ~/.config/fish/completions/).

Programmatic Invocation (CI / Ephemeral)¶

To enable completion for an ephemeral CI step (e.g., for smoke tests that rely on completion logic executing): 

crackz --show-completion bash > .crackz_comp.sh
source .crackz_comp.sh
# run tests that exercise completion

  • See the CLI Cookbook for command usage examples.
  • Visit Configuration and Advanced Performance for tuning.

Project Scope

Project Scope¶

What we're building and why

Overview¶

Crackz is a commercial AI-powered image analysis tool for detecting cracks in harbor and bridge infrastructure. It provides maritime engineers and infrastructure inspectors with automated crack detection to improve safety assessments and reduce manual inspection time.

Business Goals¶

Primary Objectives¶

  1. Automate crack detection in harbor concrete structures
  2. Reduce inspection time from manual visual inspection to automated analysis
  3. Improve detection accuracy with AI-powered segmentation models
  4. Enable enterprise deployment with Docker, GPU support, and team management
  5. Support offline operation for maritime environments with limited connectivity

Success Criteria¶

  • Detection accuracy >85% IoU on validation sets
  • Processing speed <5 seconds per image on CPU
  • Memory usage <4GB RAM for standard workflows
  • Successful deployment to 5+ customer organizations
  • 95% customer satisfaction with detection quality

Target Users¶

Primary Users¶

  1. Harbor Inspection Engineers
  2. Need: Fast, reliable crack detection for routine inspections
  3. Pain point: Manual inspection is time-consuming and subjective

  4. Success: Reduce inspection time by 60%

  5. Infrastructure Managers

  6. Need: Historical tracking of crack progression over time
  7. Pain point: Inconsistent documentation across inspections

  8. Success: Reproducible project structure with versioned results

  9. Maritime Authorities

  10. Need: Compliance reporting with standardized detection metrics
  11. Pain point: Manual report generation from inspection photos
  12. Success: Automated reporting with PDF export and GPS mapping

Secondary Users¶

  1. IT Administrators (enterprise deployment)
  2. Data Scientists (model training and tuning)
  3. Bridge Inspectors (similar use case to harbors)

Core Features (Current)¶

Project Management¶

  • ✅ Project scaffolding with reproducible directory structure
  • ✅ Image import with preprocessing (resize, organize splits)
  • ✅ Project migration for schema versioning
  • ✅ Clean command for maintenance (logs, artifacts)

AI Pipeline¶

  • ✅ Training pipeline with PyTorch Lightning
  • ✅ Detection pipeline with batch processing
  • ✅ Model checkpointing and resumption
  • ✅ TensorBoard integration for training visualization
  • ✅ Runtime overrides (epochs, batch size) without YAML edits

User Interfaces¶

  • ✅ CLI (Typer): Primary interface for automation and CI/CD
  • ✅ GUI (PySide6): Desktop app for visual project management
  • ✅ Docker: Three variants (full, slim, GPU) for enterprise deployment

Deployment & Operations¶

  • ✅ Docker images with multi-stage builds
  • ✅ Azure Batch support for distributed processing
  • ✅ Azure VM deployment scripts (CPU and GPU)
  • ✅ Hybrid logging (central + per-project)
  • ✅ GPS/EXIF support with interactive maps and GeoJSON export

Integration¶

  • ✅ MCP (Model Context Protocol) for AI assistant integration
  • ✅ Shell completion (bash, zsh, fish, PowerShell)
  • ✅ GitHub Actions CI/CD workflows
  • ✅ GitHub Copilot optimization

Features (Planned - Backlog)¶

Near-term (Next 3-6 months)¶

  • [ ] Push update solution for continuous model improvement (#282)
  • [ ] Large photo mosaic import for high-resolution scans (#215)
  • [ ] Word document report generator (complementing existing PDF export)
  • [ ] Severity classification beyond binary crack/no-crack
  • [ ] Web API for remote detection requests

Long-term (6-12 months)¶

  • [ ] Qt GUI migration for improved cross-platform support (#127)
  • [ ] Multi-model ensemble for improved accuracy
  • [ ] Active learning workflow for efficient labeling
  • [ ] Cloud-native deployment (Kubernetes, serverless)
  • [ ] Mobile app for field inspection with offline sync

Constraints¶

Technical Constraints¶

  1. Python 3.11+ minimum (3.13 recommended for performance)
  2. PyTorch ecosystem (switching ML frameworks not feasible)
  3. YAML-based config for human readability (no binary configs)
  4. Backward compatibility for project schemas (must support migration)
  5. Offline-first design (no required internet connectivity)

Performance Constraints¶

  1. Memory: Must run on laptops with 8GB RAM (4GB allocated)
  2. CPU speed: <5 seconds per image on modern Intel/AMD CPUs
  3. GPU training: Support CUDA 11.8+ and 12.x
  4. Container startup: <30 seconds cold start
  5. Test coverage: Minimum 75% (enforced in CI)

Business Constraints¶

  1. Commercial licensing: GPL-3.0 source-available model
  2. Enterprise deployment: Must support air-gapped environments
  3. Customer support: Email support within 24 hours
  4. Data privacy: No telemetry, no cloud-required features
  5. Stability: No breaking changes without major version bump

Development Constraints¶

  1. CI/CD: All tests must pass on GitHub Actions
  2. Code quality: Ruff linting, mypy type checking enforced
  3. Documentation: All public APIs must be documented
  4. Performance: No regressions >20% without justification
  5. Git workflow: No direct pushes to main, all changes via PR

Non-Goals¶

Explicitly Out of Scope¶

  1. Real-time video detection (focus on still images)
  2. 3D reconstruction (2D segmentation only)
  3. Mobile-first UI (desktop and CLI focus)
  4. Multi-user collaboration (single-user project management)
  5. Cloud storage integration (local storage only)
  6. Third-party API dependencies (self-contained operation)

Why These Are Out of Scope¶

  • Real-time video: Harbor inspections use high-res still photos, not video
  • 3D reconstruction: Not required by customers, adds complexity
  • Mobile-first: Harbor engineers use laptops/tablets with keyboards
  • Multi-user collaboration: Single inspector per project is current workflow
  • Cloud storage: Customer data privacy requirements favor local storage
  • Third-party APIs: Offline operation is critical for maritime environments

Success Metrics¶

Product Metrics¶

  • Detection Accuracy: >85% IoU on held-out test sets
  • Processing Speed: <5s per image (CPU), <1s per image (GPU)
  • Memory Usage: <4GB RAM for typical workflows
  • Crash Rate: <1% of operations (measured in telemetry opt-in)
  • Test Coverage: >75% line coverage, >80% target

Business Metrics¶

  • Customer Adoption: 10+ active customer organizations
  • User Satisfaction: 4.5+ stars (5-point scale) from customer feedback
  • Inspection Time Reduction: 50%+ reported by users
  • Support Response Time: <24 hours for email support
  • Documentation Coverage: 100% of CLI commands documented

Development Metrics¶

  • CI/CD Success Rate: >95% of runs pass
  • Release Cadence: Minor releases every 2-3 weeks
  • Issue Resolution Time: <7 days for bugs, <30 days for features
  • Code Review Time: <48 hours for PR review
  • Build Time: <10 minutes for full CI pipeline

  • Theresia Lundgren (Author, Lead Developer, Product Owner)
  • Anaxiatech AB (Development company)

External¶

  • Harbor Inspection Teams (End users, feature requests)
  • IT Administrators (Deployment, enterprise requirements)
  • Maritime Authorities (Compliance, reporting needs)
  • Bridge Inspection Companies (Adjacent market, potential expansion)

Architecture Decisions

Architecture Decisions¶

Key technical decisions and their rationale (ADR-style)

This document records important architecture decisions made during Crackz development. Each decision includes context, the decision itself, and consequences.

Format¶

Each decision follows this structure: - Context: Why we needed to make a decision - Decision: What we chose - Consequences: Trade-offs and implications - Status: Active | Deprecated | Superseded

ADR-001: Use uv for Dependency Management + hatchling for Builds¶

Context: Python package management is slow with pip and complex with poetry. Additionally, setuptools as a build backend is aging and lacks modern features.

Decision: Use a hybrid approach: - uv (Astral's package manager) for dependency management, lockfiles, and task execution - hatchling (PyPA-official build backend) for building wheels and sdists

Consequences: - ✅ 10-100x faster installs compared to pip (via uv) - ✅ Automatic virtual environment management (via uv) - ✅ Built-in lockfile support via uv.lock (deterministic builds) - ✅ Modern PEP 517-compliant build backend (hatchling) - ✅ Better build defaults (uses .gitignore for sdist) - ✅ Preserves custom PyTorch index routing (uv feature) - ✅ Compatible with python-semantic-release for versioning - ⚠️ Two tools instead of one (but clear separation of concerns) - ⚠️ Relatively new toolchain (requires team adoption)

Status: Active (Updated 2025-11-30)

Related: .github/workflows/, pyproject.toml, Dockerfile*, all documentation

Migration Notes: - Migrated from setuptools to hatchling in v0.67.0 - All existing uv configuration preserved (PyTorch routing unchanged) - Semantic versioning still managed by python-semantic-release

ADR-002: PyTorch Lightning for ML Pipeline¶

Context: Raw PyTorch requires significant boilerplate for training loops, checkpointing, and distributed training.

Decision: Use PyTorch Lightning as the ML framework layer.

Consequences: - ✅ Production-ready training with minimal boilerplate - ✅ Built-in checkpointing, logging, and callbacks - ✅ Easy GPU/multi-GPU scaling - ✅ TensorBoard integration out of the box - ⚠️ Additional abstraction layer to learn - ⚠️ Opinionated structure (less flexibility)

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/ai/training.py, src/crackz/ai/models.py

ADR-003: Typer for CLI Framework¶

Context: Need type-safe CLI with good DX, auto-generated help, and modern Python features.

Decision: Use Typer instead of Click or argparse.

Consequences: - ✅ Type hints drive CLI interface (DRY principle) - ✅ Excellent auto-generated help text - ✅ Easy to test and maintain - ✅ Built on Click (mature foundation) - ⚠️ Less flexible than raw Click for complex UIs - ⚠️ Learning curve for developers used to argparse

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/cli/, all CLI commands

ADR-004: CustomTkinter for GUI (Not Qt)¶

Context: Need lightweight desktop GUI. Qt requires commercial licensing for proprietary software; Tkinter is too basic.

Decision: Use CustomTkinter (modern Tkinter wrapper) instead of Qt or Kivy.

Consequences: - ✅ No licensing costs (compatible with GPL-3.0) - ✅ Modern dark mode support - ✅ Lightweight (~1MB vs Qt's ~50MB) - ✅ Easy to package with PyInstaller - ⚠️ Less feature-rich than Qt - ⚠️ Limited third-party widgets - ⚠️ Known issue: some customers want Qt migration (#127)

Status: Active (Qt migration under consideration)

Related: src/crackz/gui/, issue #127

ADR-005: Pydantic v2 for Configuration¶

Context: Need type-safe config validation with YAML serialization. Manual validation is error-prone.

Decision: Use Pydantic v2 models for all configuration with YAML backend.

Consequences: - ✅ Type-safe validation at load time - ✅ Auto-generated JSON schemas - ✅ Excellent error messages for invalid configs - ✅ Easy to extend and version (schema_version field) - ⚠️ YAML library dependency (pyyaml) - ⚠️ Learning curve for Pydantic's API

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/config/, project YAML files

ADR-006: Hybrid Logging Architecture¶

Context: Need system-wide logs for debugging AND per-project logs for customer audit trails.

Decision: Implement hybrid logging with: - Central log sink (pre-project operations, global context) - Per-project log sink (project-specific operations)

Consequences: - ✅ Complete audit trail per project - ✅ System-wide logging for debugging - ✅ Flexible central log location (env var, flag, or temp) - ⚠️ Slightly more complex logging setup - ⚠️ Two log locations to manage

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/log/, CRACKZ_LOG_DIR env var

ADR-007: Centralized CLI Options Pattern¶

Context: CLI option definitions were duplicated across modules (e.g., multiple FORCE_OPTION definitions).

Decision: Centralize all reusable CLI options in src/crackz/cli/options.py.

Consequences: - ✅ Single source of truth for option definitions - ✅ Consistent help text and behavior - ✅ Easy to update globally - ⚠️ Requires discipline to import (not re-define) - ⚠️ One-time refactoring effort to consolidate

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/cli/options.py, all CLI commands

ADR-008: Conventional Commits for Versioning¶

Context: Manual versioning and changelog generation is error-prone and time-consuming.

Decision: Use conventional commits (feat:, fix:, etc.) with semantic-release for automated versioning.

Consequences: - ✅ Automatic version bumps (major, minor, patch) - ✅ Auto-generated changelog from commits - ✅ Clear commit history for code review - ⚠️ Team must follow commit conventions - ⚠️ Bad commit messages affect release notes

Status: Active

Related: .releaserc.yml, GitHub Actions workflows

ADR-009: Three Docker Variants (Full, Slim, GPU)¶

Context: Different deployment scenarios need different image sizes and capabilities.

Decision: Provide three Dockerfiles: - Dockerfile: Balanced full-featured image - Dockerfile.slim: Minimal runtime (no dev tools) - Dockerfile.gpu: CUDA runtime for GPU workloads

Consequences: - ✅ Optimized images for each use case - ✅ Faster pulls for slim (smaller size) - ✅ GPU support without bloating CPU images - ⚠️ Three Dockerfiles to maintain - ⚠️ Need clear documentation on which to use

Status: Active

Related: Dockerfile, Dockerfile.slim, Dockerfile.gpu, Makefile

ADR-010: uv sync in Docker (Not Wheel Builds)¶

Context: Building wheels in Docker is slow and complex. uv sync is faster and simpler.

Decision: Use uv sync directly in Docker images instead of pre-built wheels.

Consequences: - ✅ Faster Docker builds (uv's speed) - ✅ Simpler Dockerfile (no multi-stage wheel building) - ✅ Consistent with local development workflow - ⚠️ Requires uv installed in base image - ⚠️ Build cache depends on pyproject.toml + uv.lock

Status: Active

Related: All Dockerfiles

ADR-011: Ruff for Linting and Formatting¶

Context: Traditional Python linting (flake8, black, isort) requires multiple tools and is slow.

Decision: Use Ruff for both linting and formatting (replaces black, isort, flake8, etc.).

Consequences: - ✅ 10-100x faster than traditional tools - ✅ Single tool for linting + formatting - ✅ Compatible with existing configs (black, isort rules) - ✅ Excellent VS Code integration - ⚠️ Newer tool (less mature than black) - ⚠️ Some edge cases in AST-based fixes

Status: Active

Related: pyproject.toml (Ruff config), pre-commit hooks

ADR-012: 75% Minimum Test Coverage¶

Context: Need quality gates without over-constraining development. 100% is unrealistic; <70% is too low.

Decision: Enforce 75% minimum test coverage in CI (target 85%).

Consequences: - ✅ Catches most untested code paths - ✅ Realistic target for teams - ✅ Enforced automatically in CI - ⚠️ Can be gamed with trivial tests - ⚠️ Doesn't measure test quality

Status: Active

Related: pyproject.toml (pytest-cov config), CI workflows

ADR-013: Performance Regression Tests with Benchmarks¶

Context: Performance regressions are hard to catch without automated measurement.

Decision: Use pytest-benchmark with automated regression detection (>20% mean, >30% max).

Consequences: - ✅ Catches performance regressions before merge - ✅ Historical performance tracking - ✅ Baseline updates after intentional changes - ⚠️ Benchmark stability depends on CI environment - ⚠️ Requires baseline management

Status: Active

Related: tests/unit/benchmarks/, .benchmarks/ (gitignored)

ADR-014: Project Schema Versioning with Migrations¶

Context: Project YAML format evolves over time. Breaking old projects is unacceptable for customers.

Decision: Add schema_version field to project configs with migration system.

Consequences: - ✅ Backward compatibility for customer projects - ✅ Explicit migration path for breaking changes - ✅ Safe upgrades (creates .bak files) - ⚠️ Migration code must be maintained - ⚠️ Testing migrations requires old project fixtures

Status: Active

Related: crackz migrate, src/crackz/config/, schema_version field

ADR-015: typer.secho() for User Messages, logger for Technical Info¶

Context: Mixed output methods (print, echo, console.print) created inconsistent UX.

Decision: Standardize on: - typer.secho() with colors for end-user messages - logger for technical/operational information - NEVER use print(), typer.echo(), or console.print()

Consequences: - ✅ Consistent user experience across all CLI commands - ✅ Clear separation: user messages vs operational logs - ✅ Better testability (can capture typer output) - ⚠️ Requires team discipline to follow conventions - ⚠️ One-time refactoring effort to standardize existing code

Status: Active (strictly enforced)

Related: All CLI commands, CONTRIBUTING.md, DEVELOPMENT_STANDARDS.md

ADR-016: GitHub Actions for CI/CD¶

Context: Need reliable, cloud-based CI/CD with good GitHub integration.

Decision: Use GitHub Actions exclusively (no Travis, CircleCI, etc.).

Consequences: - ✅ Native GitHub integration (PRs, issues, releases) - ✅ Free for public repos, generous for private - ✅ Good ecosystem of third-party actions - ✅ Matrix builds for multi-platform testing - ⚠️ Vendor lock-in to GitHub - ⚠️ YAML workflow syntax (learning curve)

Status: Active

Related: .github/workflows/

ADR-017: MCP (Model Context Protocol) Integration¶

Context: AI assistants (Claude, Copilot) need standardized access to development tools.

Decision: Implement MCP integration with crackz mcp init command.

Consequences: - ✅ Standardized AI assistant integration - ✅ Fine-grained permission control - ✅ Future-proof for AI-powered development - ⚠️ Relatively new protocol (evolving spec) - ⚠️ Limited ecosystem currently

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/cli/mcp_cli.py, .mcp/config.json

ADR-018: GPS/EXIF Support with GeoJSON Export¶

Context: Harbor inspections often have GPS-tagged photos. Customers need location-based reports.

Decision: Add GPS extraction from EXIF, interactive maps (Folium), and GeoJSON export.

Consequences: - ✅ Location-aware detection results - ✅ Interactive HTML maps for visual reporting - ✅ GeoJSON export for GIS integration - ⚠️ Not all images have GPS data (graceful fallback) - ⚠️ Privacy considerations (GPS data in exports)

Status: Active

Related: crackz geo commands, src/crackz/geo/

ADR-019: PySide6 Migration (Replacing CustomTkinter)¶

Context: CustomTkinter limitations became blockers for production use — limited widget set, no thread-safe state management, no native enabled/disabled widget support, customer requests for Qt (#127). A feasibility study confirmed PySide6 was viable under GPL-3.0 licensing.

Decision: Migrate GUI framework from CustomTkinter to PySide6 (Qt 6). Adopt reactive state management via QtAppState (QObject with signals) and Qt's thread-safe signal/slot mechanism via async_bridge.py.

Consequences: - ✅ Rich widget ecosystem (tree views, dock widgets, toolbars) - ✅ Native enabled/disabled widget support (setEnabled()) - ✅ Thread-safe signal/slot pattern — no manual locking for GUI state - ✅ Professional dark mode via Catppuccin Mocha QSS theming - ✅ Better packaging support (Qt deploy tools) - ⚠️ Larger dependency footprint (~50MB vs ~1MB) - ⚠️ Required full GUI rewrite (all views, dialogs, panels)

Status: Active

Related: src/crackz/gui/qt/, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-04-13-pyside6-migration-feasibility.md, supersedes ADR-004

Summary of Current Technology Stack¶

Decision Area Chosen Technology Status
Package Manager uv Active
ML Framework PyTorch Lightning Active
CLI Framework Typer Active
GUI Framework PySide6 (Qt 6) Active (replaced CustomTkinter, see ADR-019)
Configuration Pydantic v2 + YAML Active
Logging Loguru (hybrid) Active
Linting/Formatting Ruff Active
Type Checking mypy Active
Testing pytest + pytest-cov + pytest-benchmark Active
CI/CD GitHub Actions Active
Versioning semantic-release + conventional commits Active
Docker Strategy Three variants (full, slim, GPU) Active
Migration Strategy Schema versioning + crackz migrate Active
Output Standards typer.secho + logger Active (enforced)

Architecture

System Architecture¶

This document describes the current (implemented) architecture of Crackz, focusing on the actual code paths in this repository. Previous diagrams referenced future or hypothetical services (artifact stores, model servers, remote registries) that are not yet part of the codebase; those have been removed or clearly marked as future work.

High-Level Overview¶

Crackz consists of two user-facing entry points sharing a common core library: - CLI (Typer) – primary automation interface (import images, train, detect, export config) - GUI (PySide6) – exploratory desktop interface (project browsing, import, training & detection triggers, previews)

Core subsystems: - Project / Configuration: Pydantic models; YAML + env + defaults merged via pydantic-settings - Image Import & Layout: Normalizes images into split directories (raw/ train/ val/ test/) and masks - Dataset Layer: CrackzDataset (Torch Dataset) + DataLoader factory - Training & Detection Pipelines: PyTorch + PyTorch Lightning orchestration (training, validation, testing, inference) - Performance Utilities: Global seed, Trainer override extraction - Logging: Centralized through loguru with structured formatting - Artifacts & Outputs: Filesystem only (artifacts/models/, artifacts/runtime/, metrics JSON, detection PNGs)

No network services, model servers, remote registries, or cloud object storage are currently part of runtime behavior.

Open Architecture & Model Flexibility¶

Crackz is built with an open architecture that supports multiple model types and use cases:

Default Configuration: Segmentation - Binary segmentation (pixel-level classification): crack/no-crack, deviation/no-deviation - Uses U-Net architecture with configurable encoder backbones (ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet, etc.) - Suitable for: structural crack detection, surface defect analysis, damage mapping

Alternative Model Types While segmentation is the default, the architecture supports: - Classification models: Whole-image categorization (e.g., "has crack" vs "no crack") - Multi-class segmentation: Different defect types (cracks, corrosion, spalling) - Custom architectures: Bring your own PyTorch Lightning model

Model Acquisition Workflow End users have two primary paths:

  1. Train Your Own Model
  2. Import labeled training data (images + masks)
  3. Configure model architecture and training parameters
  4. Run crackz detect train to create a custom checkpoint

  5. Ideal for: domain-specific data, unique defect types, custom requirements

  6. Use Pre-Trained Models

  7. Acquire ready-made checkpoints from model providers or partners
  8. Place checkpoint in project's artifacts/models/ directory
  9. Run crackz detect run with existing checkpoint
  10. Ideal for: quick deployment, standard use cases, proof-of-concept

Encoder Flexibility The segmentation model supports any encoder from segmentation-models-pytorch, including: - ResNet family (resnet18, resnet34, resnet50, resnet101) - EfficientNet (efficientnet-b0 through efficientnet-b7) - MobileNet (mobilenet_v2) for edge deployment - DenseNet, VGG, and many others

Configure via project.yaml: 

ai:
  model:
    encoder: resnet34        # or efficientnet-b0, mobilenet_v2, etc.
    encoder_weights: imagenet # or None for random initialization

Common Use Cases & Model Examples¶

1. Harbor Infrastructure Inspection (Segmentation) - Task: Detect and map cracks in concrete harbor walls - Model: U-Net with ResNet34 encoder - Input: 512×512 grayscale or RGB images - Output: Binary segmentation mask highlighting crack pixels - Workflow: Train on labeled harbor images → Deploy for automated inspection

2. Bridge Surface Analysis (Multi-Class Segmentation) - Task: Identify different defect types (cracks, spalling, corrosion) - Model: U-Net with EfficientNet-B0 encoder, num_classes=3 - Input: High-resolution bridge deck photos - Output: Multi-class mask (class 1=crack, class 2=spalling, class 3=corrosion) - Workflow: Acquire pre-trained multi-defect model → Run detections on new structures

3. Quick Assessment (Classification) - Task: Rapid triage - does this image contain any cracks? - Model: Custom CNN classifier (future extension) - Input: Full-resolution photos - Output: Binary label (crack/no-crack) with confidence score - Workflow: Train lightweight classifier → Process thousands of images for filtering

4. Deviation Detection (Binary Segmentation) - Task: Identify surface irregularities or deviations from standard - Model: U-Net with MobileNetV2 (for edge deployment) - Input: Normalized surface scans - Output: Deviation mask - Workflow: Train on deviation examples → Deploy on mobile devices

5. Custom Domain Application - Task: Adapt to specific industry (e.g., aerospace panel inspection) - Model: Fine-tune from ImageNet pre-trained encoder - Input: Domain-specific imagery (composite materials, metal surfaces) - Output: Custom defect masks - Workflow: Collect small labeled dataset → Transfer learning → Production deployment

Evaluation & Reporting Flow¶

Detection results flow through evaluation and reporting pipelines:

flowchart LR
  A["Test Dataset"] --> B["Evaluator"]
  B --> C["Metrics Calculator"]
  C --> D["Evaluation Results"]
  D --> E["JSON/CSV Reporter"]
  D --> F["Report Generator"]
  F --> G["Branded Word Document"]
  I["Detection Results"] --> J["Visualization"]
  J --> K["Detection Overlays"]
  I --> F

Async Callback Architecture¶

Training/detection progress flows from sync threads to async GUI:

flowchart TB
  A["Training Thread (sync)"] --> B["CallbackDispatcher.sync_q"]
  B --> C["Janus Queue"]
  C --> D["CallbackDispatcher.async_q"]
  D --> E["GUI Event Loop (async)"]
  E --> F["UI Update"]

Key Features: Thread-safe sync/async bridging, backpressure handling (drops oldest on full queue), non-blocking updates.
